newsitem.title: USA: American Airlines, pilots move closer to confrontation.
newsitem.headline: American Airlines, pilots move closer to confrontation.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots moved closer to an all-out confrontation on Saturday as pilots demanded major concessions in any new labor contract and the carrier tried to push the union into binding arbitration.
Airline management said it would accept an offer of binding arbitration from the National Mediation Board (NMB), but only if pilots also agree to the offer by next Wednesday.
The Allied Pilots Association (APA), however, said it wanted more time to fix its bargaining position. On Saturday, it released a new list of demands.

The 9,300-strong APA earlier this week rejected a tentative accord which would have given pilots pay raises of 5 percent over a new four-year contract and allowed the airline to buy regional jets for its commuter carrier, American Eagle.

APA president Jim Sovich said on Saturday that the pilots were demanding pay raises of 11 percent over the life of the contract and would not allow American Eagle, which currently operates only turboprop aircraft, to fly regional jets because, he said, it would take jobs away from APA pilots.
If either side rejects binding arbitration, the National Mediation Board would then call a 30-day "cooling off" period in which there would be intensive negotiations.

At the end of the 30 days, if no agreement was struck, the APA would be free to start strike action while American Airlines, which is owned by Fort Worth, Texas-based AMR Corp., could declare a lockout or unilaterally implement new pay and work rules.
The positions effectively raised the stakes in the contract dispute.
American Airlines President Donald Carty said in a statement the pilots' rejection of the tentative labor contract was unfortunate and meant both sides should agree to binding arbitration.

But Sovich said the mediation board should have waited longer before pushing the issue of binding arbitration and had "apparently succumbed to pressure from AMR management for an early release into the 30-day cooling-off period".
He said the union had named a new negotiating committee and would formally present its fresh demands to management next Wednesday.
The APA's rejection of the tentative agreement, reached last September after two years of negotiations, effectively put American Airlines' growth plans on hold.
Only two months ago, the carrier pledged to buy 103 jets from Boeing and take out options on 527 more in one of the biggest commercial airplane orders in history.

But airline management said the Boeing deal was contingent on pilots accepting a new labor contract. The airplane order is worth about $6.5 billion at list prices and potentially as much as $35 billion.
Pilots said the labor contract was unacceptable because it offered minor wage increases and threatened pilots' jobs even as the airline is enjoying a period of record profits.

They are now demanding wage hikes of 3 percent each year in 1997, 1998 and 1999 and another 2 percent raise in the year 2000. They also want preferential options on 7.25 million AMR shares, up from the 5.75 million shares offered in the tentative agreement of last September.

AMR management will almost certainly be angered by pilots' insistence that American Eagle not be allowed to fly regional jets. Chief Executive Officer Robert Crandall had said the regional jets clause was key to American's efforts to cut costs and boost its ability to compete.
